Bún bò ở chợ Đông Ba
places.englishName: Bun bo at Dong Ba Market

pages.context: A central Saigon market name worth recognizing before you arrive because taxi drivers, hotel staff, and shoppers use the Vietnamese name.
pages.tip: Say Chợ Bến Thành as one place name; chợ simply tells you it is a market.
pages.rationale: Place-only page for market pronunciation and practice linking from shopping and route phrases.

pages.context: A pedestrian street in central Saigon that works as an easy meeting point, evening walk, or map anchor.
pages.tip: Phố đi bộ means walking street, so locals may shorten the name once the place is obvious.
pages.rationale: Street-name page supports route, stop, and meet-here practice around central Saigon.

pages.context: A major history stop in central Saigon. The Vietnamese name is short, so it is useful to learn as its own phrase.
pages.tip: Dinh means palace; keep the full name together when asking for tickets or directions.
pages.rationale: Landmark page gives standalone pronunciation and anchors ticket phrases.

pages.targetText: Nhà thờ Đức Bà Sài Gòn
pages.pronunciation: nyah thuh duk bah sai gon
pages.context: A familiar central landmark whose Vietnamese name is often easier for drivers and nearby staff than the English name alone.
pages.tip: Nhà thờ means church or cathedral; Sài Gòn keeps the landmark city-specific.
pages.rationale: Place page supports cathedral-route phrases without duplicating the generic church phrase.

pages.context: A central Saigon landmark near other sights, useful as both a visit and a meetup point.
pages.tip: Bưu điện means post office; Thành phố here points to the central city landmark.
pages.rationale: Place-only page helps users hear a practical landmark name before route phrases.

pages.context: Use this short taxi or walking-map phrase when Ben Thanh Market is the destination.
pages.tip: It is intentionally clipped, which is fine when you are pointing at a map or already in a ride.
pages.rationale: Beginner route phrase naturally emerges from the market place page.

pages.context: Use this when you are nearby but need a person to point you toward the market entrance or street.
pages.tip: Keep the place name first, then ở đâu for where; that frame works for many city landmarks.
pages.rationale: Question frame teaches a reusable city-specific way to ask for a landmark.

pages.targetText: Dừng ở phố đi bộ Nguyễn Huệ
pages.englishText: Stop at Nguyen Hue Walking Street
pages.pronunciation: zoong uh foh dee boh ngween hweh
pages.context: Use this in a car or taxi when the walking street is where you want to get out.
pages.tip: Dừng ở is a useful stop-here frame; the long place name does the specific work.
pages.rationale: Beginner stop phrase ties the street-name page to a real ride moment.

pages.targetText: Phố đi bộ Nguyễn Huệ gần đây không?
pages.englishText: Is Nguyen Hue Walking Street near here?
pages.pronunciation: foh dee boh ngween hweh gun day khong
pages.context: Use this before walking when you want a quick yes/no check about distance.
pages.tip: Gần đây không is a compact near-here question that works well with a map open.
pages.rationale: Beginners need a short distance check before committing to a walk.

pages.targetText: Một vé vào Dinh Độc Lập
pages.pronunciation: mot veh vow zin dok lup
pages.context: Use this at the ticket counter when you only need one entry ticket.
pages.tip: Một vé vào is a reusable attraction frame; swap the landmark after it.
pages.rationale: Ticket phrase follows naturally from the Independence Palace page.

pages.targetText: Đi Nhà thờ Đức Bà Sài Gòn
pages.pronunciation: dee nyah thuh duk bah sai gon
pages.context: Use this with a driver or when confirming a walking route to the cathedral area.
pages.tip: The long landmark name is okay; say it slowly and show the map at the same time.
pages.rationale: A place page needs its simplest go-to sentence for beginner travel flow.
chunks: Nhà thờ Đức Bà Sài Gòn

pages.targetText: Bưu điện Thành phố ở đâu?
pages.englishText: Where is the Central Post Office?
pages.pronunciation: boo deen tahn foh uh dow
pages.context: Use this around the cathedral and central streets when you want someone to point you toward the post office landmark.
pages.tip: The place name plus ở đâu keeps the sentence short and useful for asking strangers.
pages.rationale: Landmark-specific where question for a common central Saigon stop.

pages.englishText: Let me get off in District 1
pages.pronunciation: choh toy swoong uh kwun mot
pages.context: Use this in a ride when District 1 is close enough and you want to stop there.
pages.tip: Cho tôi xuống ở is useful but a little longer, so show the map pin too.
pages.rationale: District 1 is a natural route anchor for first-time Saigon travelers.

pages.context: Use this as a quick orientation check when a hotel, cafe, or driver mentions District 1.
pages.tip: District names are practical in Saigon; learning Quận 1 pays off immediately.
pages.rationale: Short neighborhood-distance check for first-time city orientation.

pages.targetText: Có nhà thuốc gần chợ Bến Thành không?
pages.englishText: Is there a pharmacy near Ben Thanh Market?
pages.pronunciation: koh nyah thwok gun chuh ben tahn khong
pages.context: Use this when you need medicine or a small health item while shopping near Ben Thanh.
pages.tip: Có ... gần ... không asks whether something exists near a known place.
pages.rationale: Practical-help phrase stays city-specific by anchoring the pharmacy need to a landmark.

pages.targetText: Có ATM gần phố đi bộ Nguyễn Huệ không?
pages.englishText: Is there an ATM near Nguyen Hue Walking Street?
pages.pronunciation: koh ay tee em gun foh dee boh ngween hweh khong
pages.context: Use this before shopping, eating, or meeting friends near the walking street.
pages.tip: ATM is commonly understood; keep the landmark clear so the answer is nearby, not citywide.
pages.rationale: Money-help phrase with a strong city place anchor.

pages.targetText: Tôi muốn đến Dinh Độc Lập
pages.englishText: I want to go to Independence Palace
pages.pronunciation: toy moon den zin dok lup
pages.context: Use this at a hotel desk or with a driver when you need help getting to the palace.
pages.tip: Tôi muốn đến is a gentle I-want-to-go-to frame that sounds more complete than just naming the place.
pages.rationale: Adds a polite route request for a major landmark without becoming too long.

pages.targetText: Đi đường Đồng Khởi được không?
pages.englishText: Can we go by Dong Khoi Street?
pages.pronunciation: dee duong dong khoi duoc khong
pages.context: Use this if you want a route that passes a central street you recognize from your map.
pages.tip: Đường means street; được không asks whether the route is possible.
pages.rationale: Street-specific route phrase prepares the library for map-based practice.

pages.context: Use this when deciding whether a market trip makes sense from where you are.
pages.tip: Xa không is a short far-or-not check; expect a gesture, number, or ride suggestion.
pages.rationale: Market phrase adds a second Saigon market without making a duplicate Ben Thanh page.

pages.targetText: Cho tôi đến Bưu điện Thành phố
pages.englishText: Please take me to the Central Post Office
pages.pronunciation: choh toy den boo deen tahn foh
pages.context: Use this with a driver when the post office is the destination or nearby landmark.
pages.tip: Cho tôi đến is a polite take-me-to frame for taxis and ride pickups.
pages.rationale: Route phrase extends the post office place page into a practical ride request.

pages.targetText: Tôi muốn mua SIM gần chợ Bến Thành
pages.englishText: I want to buy a SIM near Ben Thanh Market
pages.pronunciation: toy moon mua sim gun chuh ben tahn
pages.context: Use this if you are already around the market and need mobile data before moving on.
pages.tip: The phrase asks for the errand and the place anchor in one sentence.
pages.rationale: Phone-help phrase is city-specific and useful during first arrival days.

pages.targetText: Nhà hàng Anăn Sài Gòn ở đâu?
pages.pronunciation: nyah hang ah nan sai gon uh dow
pages.context: Use this when a specific restaurant booking or food plan is already part of your Saigon itinerary.
pages.tip: Nhà hàng means restaurant; keep the restaurant name exact and show the address if needed.
pages.rationale: City food phrase adds a real named restaurant with clear source provenance.

pages.targetText: Tôi có đặt bàn ở Anăn Sài Gòn
pages.englishText: I have a reservation at Anan Saigon
pages.pronunciation: toy koh dat ban uh ah nan sai gon
pages.context: Use this at the restaurant entrance when staff need to find an existing reservation.
pages.tip: This is a rarer advanced page because bookings require more exact wording; show the booking name right away.
pages.rationale: One high-value restaurant booking phrase per city gives advanced users a real use case.

pages.context: Use this for a simple route to the backpacker nightlife street area.
pages.tip: Say the full street name and show the map; it is short enough for a beginner to repeat.
pages.rationale: Street-specific beginner page supports tourist nightlife navigation.

pages.context: Use this clipped phrase when confirming a hotel area or showing a hotel address in District 1.
pages.tip: It is not a full sentence, but it works well with a booking screen or map.
pages.rationale: Beginners often need area confirmation before they can form full hotel questions.

pages.context: A central Hanoi lake and orientation point. Learn the Vietnamese name because it appears in directions, cafes, walks, and hotel advice.
pages.tip: Hồ means lake; keep Hoàn Kiếm together as the proper name.
pages.rationale: Place-only page anchors Hanoi walking, meeting, coffee, and direction phrases.

pages.context: A core first-time traveler area in Hanoi. The Vietnamese name helps with hotels, pickup points, and walking directions.
pages.tip: Phố cổ means old quarter or old streets; Hà Nội makes the place specific.
pages.rationale: Place page supports city-specific neighborhood and hotel phrases.

pages.context: A major Hanoi landmark with a short Vietnamese name that is useful for tickets and rides.
pages.tip: The English name is long, but Văn Miếu is compact and practical.
pages.rationale: Place page teaches the local landmark name before route and ticket phrases.

pages.context: A well-known Hanoi market name travelers may hear around the Old Quarter.
pages.tip: Chợ marks it as a market, so it pairs naturally with shopping and nearby-help phrases.
pages.rationale: Place-only market page gives Hanoi shopping practice a real anchor.

pages.context: A recognizable Old Quarter street name useful for evening plans, meetup points, and simple taxi routes.
pages.tip: Phố means street; say the name slowly and show the map if it is noisy.
pages.rationale: Street-name page prepares city-specific practice for nightlife and route questions.

pages.context: Use this with a driver or when pointing to the lake on a map.
pages.tip: The frame is short and city-specific; the place name carries the important information.
pages.rationale: Beginner route phrase naturally follows the lake place page.

pages.context: Use this when you are close to the Old Quarter and need someone to point the lake direction.
pages.tip: Place name plus ở đâu is one of the most reusable city question frames.
pages.rationale: Where question anchors the lake as a first-time traveler reference point.

pages.targetText: Phố cổ Hà Nội gần đây không?
pages.englishText: Is Hanoi Old Quarter near here?
pages.pronunciation: foh koh ha noy gun day khong
pages.context: Use this when checking whether you can walk to the Old Quarter from a cafe, hotel, or station.
pages.tip: Gần đây không invites a yes/no answer, a pointing gesture, or a time estimate.
pages.rationale: Short near-here phrase helps travelers decide whether to walk.

pages.englishText: Go to the Temple of Literature
pages.context: Use this as the simplest route phrase to the Temple of Literature.
pages.tip: The Vietnamese landmark name is short, so it is a strong beginner phrase.
pages.rationale: Basic route phrase links the place page to a real sightseeing route.

pages.englishText: One ticket to the Temple of Literature
pages.context: Use this at the entrance when asking for a single ticket.
pages.tip: Một vé vào is a simple attraction-counter frame.
pages.rationale: Ticket phrase builds from the same landmark without creating a generic ticket page.

pages.context: Use this in or near the Old Quarter when looking for the market.
pages.tip: If the answer is a gesture, follow it first and ask again when closer.
pages.rationale: Market-specific question gives shopping practice a Hanoi anchor.

pages.context: Use this for a simple route to a familiar Old Quarter evening street.
pages.tip: In busy nightlife areas, show the map pin while saying the street name.
pages.rationale: Street route phrase adds a real Hanoi nightlife landmark without generic wording.

pages.targetText: Dừng ở phố cổ Hà Nội
pages.pronunciation: zoong uh foh koh ha noy
pages.context: Use this in a car when the Old Quarter is the drop-off area.
pages.tip: For exact hotels, follow this phrase with the booking screen or address.
pages.rationale: Drop-off phrase supports arrivals and ride navigation in Hanoi.

pages.targetText: Có cà phê trứng gần hồ Hoàn Kiếm không?
pages.englishText: Is there egg coffee near Hoan Kiem Lake?
pages.pronunciation: koh kah feh trung gun hoh hwan keem khong
pages.context: Use this when you want a Hanoi-specific coffee stop near the lake.
pages.tip: Cà phê trứng is egg coffee; anchor it near the lake so the answer is practical.
pages.rationale: Food phrase is city-specific and useful before arrival because egg coffee is a Hanoi bucket-list item.

pages.targetText: Quán cà phê Giảng ở đâu?
pages.pronunciation: kwan kah feh zang uh dow
pages.context: Use this when looking for the named cafe rather than asking generally for coffee.
pages.tip: Quán cà phê means cafe; the proper name makes the question city-specific.
pages.rationale: Named cafe phrase supports real itinerary practice with a specific Hanoi anchor.

pages.targetText: Đi Nhà hát Múa rối Thăng Long
pages.englishText: Go to Thang Long Water Puppet Theatre
pages.pronunciation: dee nyah hat moo-ah zoi thang long
pages.context: Use this for a specific Hanoi show venue near the lake area.
pages.tip: The phrase is longer because the venue name is long; show the address and say it slowly.
pages.rationale: A cultural-attraction route phrase gives Hanoi more than market and lake practice.

pages.targetText: Cho tôi xuống ở hồ Hoàn Kiếm
pages.englishText: Let me get off at Hoan Kiem Lake
pages.pronunciation: choh toy swoong uh hoh hwan keem
pages.context: Use this in a ride when the lake is the drop-off landmark.
pages.tip: Cho tôi xuống is useful when you are already moving and want a clear stopping point.
pages.rationale: Ride phrase turns the lake place page into a practical drop-off command.

pages.targetText: Có ATM gần phố cổ Hà Nội không?
pages.englishText: Is there an ATM near Hanoi Old Quarter?
pages.pronunciation: koh ay tee em gun foh koh ha noy khong
pages.context: Use this when you need cash before eating, shopping, or taking a ride in the Old Quarter.
pages.tip: ATM plus a neighborhood anchor makes the request easier than asking for any ATM in Hanoi.
pages.rationale: Practical-help phrase uses an actual Hanoi area, not generic ATM wording.

pages.targetText: Có nhà thuốc gần chợ Đồng Xuân không?
pages.englishText: Is there a pharmacy near Dong Xuan Market?
pages.pronunciation: koh nyah thwok gun chuh dong swun khong
pages.context: Use this when a health need comes up during market or Old Quarter time.
pages.tip: The landmark keeps the answer local and actionable.
pages.rationale: Practical medical errand remains city-specific through the market anchor.

pages.targetText: Tôi muốn mua quà ở Hàng Gai
pages.englishText: I want to buy gifts on Hang Gai
pages.pronunciation: toy moon mua kwah uh hang gai
pages.context: Use this when asking hotel staff or a driver about shopping around Hang Gai Street.
pages.tip: Mua quà means buy gifts; the street anchor keeps the phrase from being generic shopping talk.
pages.rationale: Shopping phrase teaches a useful errand around a named Hanoi street.

pages.englishText: Can we go to the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum?
pages.context: Use this when checking a route or ride to the mausoleum area.
pages.tip: Lăng Bác is a common Vietnamese way to refer to the mausoleum; được không asks if the plan is possible.
pages.rationale: Landmark route phrase adds a major Hanoi site with natural local naming.

pages.targetText: Từ đây đến Văn Miếu bao lâu?
pages.englishText: How long from here to the Temple of Literature?
pages.pronunciation: tuh day den van mee-ew bao low
pages.context: Use this before committing to a walk, taxi, or next sightseeing stop.
pages.tip: Từ đây đến ... bao lâu asks travel time from your current place.
pages.rationale: Intermediate route-timing frame is high value for city days.

pages.targetText: Tôi có đặt bàn ở Tầm Vị
pages.englishText: I have a reservation at Tam Vi
pages.pronunciation: toy koh dat ban uh tum vee
pages.context: Use this at a named restaurant when staff need to find an existing booking.
pages.tip: Keep the booking name visible; this phrase just tells staff what kind of record to look for.
pages.rationale: One advanced named-restaurant reservation page gives Hanoi a realistic booking use case.

pages.context: Use this in the Old Quarter when a shop, hotel, or walking route names Hang Bac Street.
pages.tip: Street names can be hard by ear; repeat phố plus the name and show the map if needed.
pages.rationale: Adds a second Old Quarter street for place-name practice.

pages.context: Use this when heading to the bridge area as a landmark or photo stop.
pages.tip: Cầu means bridge; that same word appears in many city directions.
pages.rationale: Bridge phrase expands Hanoi landmark practice beyond the lake and Old Quarter.

pages.context: A major Da Nang beach name that works for rides, hotels, walking plans, and food nearby.
pages.tip: Biển means beach or sea; Mỹ Khê is the place name.
pages.rationale: Place-only beach page anchors Da Nang route and practice flows.

pages.context: A highly recognizable Da Nang bridge name and easy navigation anchor along the river.
pages.tip: Cầu means bridge; Rồng means dragon.
pages.rationale: Place page supports bridge-specific route, ATM, and river phrases.

pages.context: A key Da Nang attraction name worth learning before you ask for tickets or travel time.
pages.tip: The Vietnamese name does not sound like the English translation, so practice it as a place name.
pages.rationale: Landmark page gives a specific attraction pronunciation for sightseeing pages.

pages.context: A nature area and route destination in Da Nang. The name is useful with drivers and tour desks.
pages.tip: Bán đảo means peninsula; Sơn Trà is the local name.
pages.rationale: Nature-place page supports route and pagoda questions tied to Son Tra.

pages.context: A central Da Nang market name useful for shopping, food, and nearby-help phrases.
pages.tip: Chợ tells you this is a market; Hàn ties it to the river/city name.
pages.rationale: Place-only market page anchors shopping and practical-help practice.

pages.context: Use this with a driver or hotel desk when the beach is your destination.
pages.tip: Beach names are common route anchors in Da Nang, so this short phrase is practical.
pages.rationale: Simple beach route phrase follows directly from the place page.

pages.targetText: Biển Mỹ Khê gần đây không?
pages.englishText: Is My Khe Beach near here?
pages.pronunciation: byen mee kheh gun day khong
pages.context: Use this before walking or choosing a ride from your hotel area.
pages.tip: The answer may be a time or a direction; show your map if you need a clearer next step.
pages.rationale: Distance-check frame is beginner-friendly and tied to a real Da Nang beach.

pages.context: Use this when Dragon Bridge is your route destination or meeting point.
pages.tip: Cầu Rồng is short and very useful for city orientation.
pages.rationale: Bridge route phrase links the place page to a common first-time traveler stop.

pages.context: Use this when you are near the river and want someone to point out the bridge direction.
pages.tip: Because the place name is short, this is a clean starter question.
pages.rationale: Where question gives the bridge page a practical search-and-find use.

pages.targetText: Một vé vào Ngũ Hành Sơn
pages.pronunciation: mot veh vow ngoo hanh son
pages.context: Use this at an entrance or ticket counter for the Marble Mountains.
pages.tip: Một vé vào is a reusable attraction phrase; the local name is the part to practice.
pages.rationale: Ticket page gives a concrete attraction-counter moment.

pages.context: Use this in a ride when the market is where you want to get out.
pages.tip: Dừng ở plus a place name is one of the easiest ride phrases to reuse.
pages.rationale: Market page needs a drop-off phrase for taxis and rides.

pages.context: Use this when looking for the market from a river walk, cafe, or hotel.
pages.tip: The phrase is short and can be paired with a pointing gesture.
pages.rationale: Shopping phrase teaches a city-specific market name with the reusable where frame.

pages.context: Use this with a driver or tour desk when Son Tra is the destination area.
pages.tip: This is place-name heavy; show the map to avoid confusion with a specific stop inside Son Tra.
pages.rationale: Nature route page adds a Da Nang-specific destination beyond the beach.

pages.context: Use this when you are already planning a Son Tra visit and need the pagoda direction.
pages.tip: Chùa means pagoda; it helps locals know this is the religious landmark.
pages.rationale: Pagoda question creates a natural child page from the Son Tra lesson.

pages.targetText: Có nhà thuốc gần chợ Hàn không?
pages.englishText: Is there a pharmacy near Han Market?
pages.pronunciation: koh nyah thwok gun chuh han khong
pages.context: Use this when you need a small health item while shopping or walking in central Da Nang.
pages.tip: The market anchor makes the help request local and actionable.
pages.rationale: Practical-help page remains city-specific with a real market anchor.

pages.targetText: Có ATM gần cầu Rồng không?
pages.englishText: Is there an ATM near Dragon Bridge?
pages.pronunciation: koh ay tee em gun cow zong khong
pages.context: Use this before river walking, food stops, or market shopping near Dragon Bridge.
pages.tip: Keep the landmark in the phrase so the answer is nearby, not across the city.
pages.rationale: Money-help phrase maps a real Da Nang landmark to a practical need.

pages.context: Use this when a riverfront route or address mentions Bach Dang Street.
pages.tip: Đường means street; it is helpful when reading addresses aloud.
pages.rationale: Street-specific page prepares users for Da Nang map and address practice.

pages.targetText: Sân bay Đà Nẵng ở đâu?
pages.pronunciation: sun bay da nang uh dow
pages.context: Use this when orienting arrival or departure plans in the city.
pages.tip: Sân bay means airport; adding Đà Nẵng keeps it city-specific.
pages.rationale: Airport phrase supports onboarding and city route filters.

pages.targetText: Cho tôi xuống ở biển Mỹ Khê
pages.englishText: Let me get off at My Khe Beach
pages.pronunciation: choh toy swoong uh byen mee kheh
pages.context: Use this in a ride when the beach area is the drop-off point.
pages.tip: If your hotel is nearby, show the address after saying the beach phrase.
pages.rationale: Beach drop-off phrase is realistic for first-time Da Nang arrivals.

pages.targetText: Từ đây đến Ngũ Hành Sơn bao lâu?
pages.englishText: How long from here to Marble Mountains?
pages.pronunciation: tuh day den ngoo hanh son bao low
pages.context: Use this to decide whether the attraction fits your current day plan.
pages.tip: Từ đây đến ... bao lâu asks travel time from right where you are.
pages.rationale: Intermediate timing page helps travelers plan city sightseeing realistically.

pages.targetText: Tôi muốn ăn hải sản ở biển Mỹ Khê
pages.englishText: I want seafood at My Khe Beach
pages.pronunciation: toy moon an hai san uh byen mee kheh
pages.context: Use this when asking a hotel, driver, or local helper for a seafood place near the beach.
pages.tip: Hải sản means seafood; the beach anchor keeps the request local.
pages.rationale: Food phrase is tied to a Da Nang beach area rather than generic ordering.

pages.targetText: Nhà hàng Nén Đà Nẵng ở đâu?
pages.englishText: Where is Nen Da Nang restaurant?
pages.pronunciation: nyah hang nen da nang uh dow
pages.context: Use this if a named restaurant is already in your plan and you need help finding it.
pages.tip: Nhà hàng identifies it as a restaurant; the city name avoids confusion with other branches or names.
pages.rationale: Named restaurant phrase adds a real Da Nang food anchor without broad claims.

pages.targetText: Tôi có đặt bàn ở Nén Đà Nẵng
pages.englishText: I have a reservation at Nen Da Nang
pages.pronunciation: toy koh dat ban uh nen da nang
pages.context: Use this at the restaurant entrance when staff need to find an existing booking.
pages.tip: Show the booking screen so staff can match the name, time, and party size.
pages.rationale: One advanced reservation page gives the city food lane a precise high-value phrase.

pages.context: Use this when you want the riverfront walking area rather than a single bridge.
pages.tip: Bờ sông means riverbank or riverfront; it is useful for walking directions.
pages.rationale: Riverfront phrase expands Da Nang beyond single landmarks.

pages.targetText: Cho tôi đến sân bay Đà Nẵng
pages.englishText: Please take me to Da Nang Airport
pages.pronunciation: choh toy den sun bay da nang
pages.context: Use this with a driver when leaving for the airport.
pages.tip: This is a complete ride phrase and still short enough for beginners.
pages.rationale: Airport departure phrase completes the Da Nang arrivals-route set.

pages.context: The core Hoi An visit area and a phrase worth knowing before hotel, ticket, and walking questions.
pages.tip: Phố cổ means old town; Hội An keeps the phrase city-specific.
pages.rationale: Place-only page anchors many Hoi An route and ticket phrases.

pages.context: A short Vietnamese landmark name for one of Hoi An's most recognizable sights.
pages.tip: Chùa means pagoda and cầu means bridge; together they name the landmark.
pages.rationale: Place page helps users hear the local name before asking directions.

pages.context: A beach name travelers may use for ride, food, and hotel questions around Hoi An.
pages.tip: Biển means beach; An Bàng is the proper name.
pages.rationale: Beach place page supports route and time phrases outside the old town.

pages.context: A practical market name for food, shopping, ATM, and help-nearby phrases.
pages.tip: Chợ plus the city name is simple and useful.
pages.rationale: Place-only market page creates a real anchor for Hoi An errands.

pages.context: A named Hoi An food stop many travelers may put on a food walk list.
pages.tip: Bánh mì is the food; Phượng is the proper name.
pages.rationale: Named food-place page supports pronunciation practice and route phrases.

pages.englishText: Go to Hoi An Ancient Town
pages.context: Use this with a driver or hotel desk when the old town is the destination.
pages.tip: The old town name is the core anchor; show your hotel or ticket screen if needed.
pages.rationale: Beginner route phrase builds directly from the Ancient Town place page.

pages.targetText: Phố cổ Hội An ở đâu?
